title: An Ebola Outbreak That Could Rival the Worst
hook: The 2026 Ebola outbreak in DR Congo has passed 5,000 cases and 2,378 deaths — the fastest fatal spread in Ebola's recorded history, still outpacing the response.
key_points: An Ebola outbreak is spreading in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda.
Early CDC modeling projected more than 20,000 cases in three months without immediate action.
By mid-August the outbreak had recorded 5,021 cases and 2,378 deaths — infecting and killing more people, faster, than any Ebola outbreak in history.
The WHO says 80% of new Congo cases come from chains of transmission that can't be traced — the outbreak is outrunning tracking efforts.
DR Congo is training 21,000 people to help trace and contain cases as the spread eludes officials.
The strain behind this outbreak never had a treatment designed for it — but three clinical trials are now testing options built specifically for it.
content_html: A new Ebola outbreak is spreading in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, and a CDC analysis suggested it could become very serious. According to NPR, early modeling projected that without immediate action, the outbreak could sicken more than 20,000 people over three months — a toll that would rival the worst Ebola outbreaks ever recorded.
extra_html:
The modeling was really a warning about choices, not a fixed prediction: Ebola spreads through contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, so outbreaks grow or shrink depending on how fast responders can find cases, trace contacts, and safely isolate the sick.

As of July 20, Congo's health ministry reported the death toll had passed 930, out of 2,344 confirmed cases, with 37 deaths recorded in a single 24-hour period — one of the highest daily tolls of the outbreak, per the Associated Press. New suspected cases have continued to turn up in parts of Congo beyond the original epicenter in Ituri, and the World Health Organization has said 80% of new cases in eastern Congo are now emerging from chains of transmission that can't be traced back to a known source — a sign the outbreak has been spreading faster than health officials can track it.

By July 23, NPR reported the death toll had surpassed 1,000 — out of roughly 2,500 recorded cases — making this the fastest fatal surge in Ebola's recorded history, with the outbreak still eluding officials trying to predict where it would spread next. In response, DR Congo is training some 21,000 people to help find cases, trace contacts, and get a firmer grasp on the spread — a scale of mobilization that reflects how hard this outbreak has been to track.

There's a hopeful note, too: the specific viral strain behind this outbreak has never had a treatment or preventive measure designed for it, but three new clinical trials are now underway testing options built for this exact strain — the first real chance at something tailored to the virus doctors are actually fighting.

By August 19, government data put the outbreak at 5,021 cases and 2,378 deaths, per the Associated Press — meaning it has now infected and killed more people at greater speed than any Ebola outbreak on record, and is still outpacing the response mounted against it.

flashcards.prompt: What did CDC modeling project if the 2026 Ebola outbreak isn't contained quickly?
flashcards.back_html: More than 20,000 cases within three months — a scale that would rival the worst Ebola outbreaks on record. The modeling stresses that immediate action is what determines how large it gets.

flashcards.prompt: Where is the 2026 Ebola outbreak in this report centered?

choices.text: The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda
West Africa: Liberia and Sierra Leone

flashcards.explanation_html: The outbreak described is in the DR Congo and Uganda. (West Africa was the site of the record 2014–16 outbreak — a different event.)

flashcards.prompt: Why do the new clinical trials matter, beyond just being 'more research'?
flashcards.back_html: The strain driving this outbreak has never had a treatment or preventive measure designed specifically for it. The three new trials are the first real shot at changing that, as the outbreak continues to spread beyond its original epicenter.

flashcards.prompt: What does the WHO say about 80% of new cases in eastern Congo?

choices.text: They come from transmission chains that can't be traced to a known source
They're all linked back to a single confirmed source
They occurred in health workers only

flashcards.explanation_html: Untraceable transmission chains mean responders can't find and isolate the source of most new cases — a sign the outbreak is spreading faster than it can be tracked.
